extracted.intended_audience: empirical legal scholars, patent litigators, judges, and policymakers interested in patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and doctrinal analysis of modern patent litigation outcomes (summary judgment, claim construction, invalidity grounds, trials) and the procedural and substantive legal standards that shape those outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard ('insolubly ambiguous')
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current Federal Circuit law, a claim is indefinite only if it is 'insolubly ambiguous.' Indefiniteness is treated as a pure question of law normally decided in connection with claim construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness is often decided during claim construction; some indefiniteness rulings may be embedded inside claim-construction orders and not styled as summary judgment. The Federal Circuit has been hostile to expansive indefiniteness findings, but the Supreme Court (e.g., Nautilus) may broaden the doctrine. Practitioners should accordingly watch claim-draft clarity and expect courts to address definiteness at the claim-construction stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function / software claims: algorithm disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For means-plus-function limitations in software patents, courts require disclosure of the corresponding structure — typically an algorithm — in the specification; absent adequate algorithm disclosure, the claim may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited (Function Media, ePlus, Noah, Ergo, Typhoon Touch, In re Aoyama, Aristocrat, WMS Gaming) explain that the specification must disclose the algorithm or corresponding structure performing the claimed function. The disclosed structure need not be software code verbatim (Typhoon), but must show a 'step-by-step process' for reaching the result. Failure to disclose sufficient algorithmic structure can render a means-plus-function claim indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction as prerequisite to substantive summary judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction (Markman) is usually a prerequisite to most substantive rulings in a patent case (validity and infringement), because the construed scope of the claim determines many summary-judgment issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markman requires courts to decide claim construction as a matter of law, typically during a pretrial 'Markman hearing.' Because claim construction precedes many summary-judgment motions, courts often resolve claim terms first; claims that cannot be construed may give rise to indefiniteness rulings as part of that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of summary judgment of validity (often single-ground rulings)
rubrics_metrics.description: A motion for summary judgment of validity frequently addresses a single ground (for example, anticipation), and even a granted motion may not preclude the opponent from contesting validity on different grounds (e.g., enablement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret summary-judgment-of-validity wins conservatively: a granted SJ on one ground does not necessarily mean the patent is fully upheld against all invalidity defenses. Empirical counts should therefore note the ground-specific nature of many SJ rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric burdens for summary judgment (patentee vs accused infringer)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain summary judgment of infringement, a patentee must show a lack of disputed issues of material fact for all elements of the claimed invention; an accused infringer seeking summary judgment of noninfringement need only show a lack of disputed issues of material fact for any single element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This asymmetry makes SJ more available and advantageous to accused infringers: defendants can move on one or more discrete bases and need only negate one element. Plaintiffs (patentees) face a higher burden at the SJ stage and must clear every element to obtain SJ of infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractioning of patent law: patentee must win every issue
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee typically must prevail on every substantive issue presented (validity, infringement, inequitable conduct, etc.) to win the case; losing even a single issue can result in losing the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because cases often present multiple, independent defenses, defendants can win by prevailing on any one. This multiplicity of possible defenses (‘fractioning’) advantages accused infringers and explains why split decisions generally favor defendants. Strategic implication: patentees face higher aggregate risk across multiple issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical success rates of invalidity summary-judgment motions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the authors' dataset, accused infringers prevailed on only about 31% of invalidity summary-judgment motions overall; motions alleging lack of patentable subject matter were the only category to prevail a majority of the time (14 of 26, or 54%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other common categories—prior art (section 102), obviousness (section 103), and section 112 issues—had substantially lower SJ success rates (patentees defeated these motions more than four times in five). The dataset treats split rulings as separate observations; robustness checks that reweighted splits did not materially change the ~31% figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial outcomes vs pretrial rulings (patentees fare better at trial)
rubrics_metrics.description: When cases reached trial in the dataset, patentees prevailed in approximately 60.7% of trials (59.4% of jury-decided patents; 63.9% of bench-decided patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many cases settle after denials of summary judgment and before trial, trial-win rates reflect a selected subset of disputes; selection and settlement effects mean SJ-stage statistics and trial statistics must be interpreted together when assessing patentee success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and settlement bias in patent litigation data
rubrics_metrics.description: Less than 10% of patent lawsuits filed in 2008–2009 resulted in any merits decision in the dataset (462 of ~5,029); more than 90% settle before summary judgment or trial, and many settlements are confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because settlements (often confidential) remove cases from the pool that reach merits decisions, published merits-outcome statistics are subject to selection bias. Researchers and readers should interpret outcome rates with caution given possible unobserved differences between settled and litigated cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forum shopping and district-specific outcome variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The district in which a case is litigated correlates with different win rates: the Eastern District of Texas and District of Delaware (and SDNY) were significantly more likely to rule for patentees in this dataset, while the Central District of California was significantly less likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are correlations from multivariate regressions that control for patent, patentee, technology, and industry characteristics; they do not prove causation. Potential confounders include case selection (stronger/weaker cases filed in particular districts) and differences in settlement propensity or case pendency. Forum choice can materially affect cases that reach merits decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting rules for observations and robustness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The study treated split rulings as separate observations in the main analysis but also reweighted observations as a robustness check; reweighting did not materially change the key win-rate statistics (e.g., patentee win rate remained ~26% on definitive merits rulings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses of litigation should state clearly how split rulings and multi-patent cases are counted and should report robustness checks (e.g., reweighting) because counting choices can affect measured rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical methods for analyzing binary litigation outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logistic (logit) regression models for binary outcomes, cluster standard errors on unique patent numbers to account for nonindependence among observations, and apply bootstrapping to control for false discovery rates when running multiple tests across outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors describe a specific bootstrap procedure (resampling the 949 observations fifty times, running separate logits for each resample, averaging coefficients) and clustering on patent numbers to address dependence among observations (multiple patents per case, same patent in multiple suits, consolidations). Empirical researchers should adopt similar techniques to mitigate correlated observations and multiple-testing problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rise of indefiniteness challenges linked to software patents and claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness challenges have grown in prevalence—now a large category of adjudicated challenges—partly because many decisions in the dataset involve software patents and because the Federal Circuit applied indefiniteness more vigorously to software means-plus-function claims; claim construction itself has become common and invites indefiniteness rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners litigating software patents should anticipate more indefiniteness attacks, particularly on means-plus-function claim language, and should ensure the specification discloses sufficient structure/algorithmic detail. Empirical counts of indefiniteness may understate true prevalence because some indefiniteness rulings occur as part of claim-construction orders.
